title: Greedy Best-First Finds Fast Paths in Reykjavík!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First race across a realistic street-map grid to reach a goal with minimal exploration. The animation reveals how the heuristic steers decisions when every node has a “promising” score.
ig_caption:
🧭✨ Reykjavík streets, one heuristic at a time!

In this visualization we run **Greedy Best-First**: at every step, the algorithm expands the node that looks **closest to the goal** (based on an estimated cost/heuristic), not the full true path cost. In graph terms, each intersection/segment becomes a node/edge, and the search is driven by an **h(n) = estimated distance-to-target** ranking—often speeding up solutions but risking suboptimal routes if the heuristic misleads. ❄️🌍

Using a real-world style street graph (think weighted edges approximating travel distance), the priority queue repeatedly selects the most “promising” frontier node. ⚡📍

Want to see how different heuristics change the route quality on the same map? Comment your favorite heuristic (Euclidean, Manhattan, or custom) and follow for more pathfinding deep-dives! 🚀
fb_caption:
🚦 Greedy Best-First is searching the map! 

This video visualizes a classic graph search approach: we treat street networks as graphs (nodes = intersections, edges = road segments) and use a heuristic to choose which frontier node to expand next. Share this with a friend who loves algorithms—and tell me if you think a “closest-to-goal” strategy will always find the best route! ✅
yt_description:
Greedy Best-First pathfinding visualization in Reykjavík (Vesturbær)! Watch how the priority queue always expands the node with the smallest heuristic distance to the goal. 🧠✨

In this Shorts-style demo, we model a real street map as a graph (intersections + road connections) and compare the mechanics of heuristic-driven search vs. exploring blindly.
